The movement of tens of thousands of people from the Mirpur district of Pakistani-administered Kashmir to Britain, which grew sharply from about 1960.

Men from Mirpur had worked as stokers on British steamships since the 19th century, and a few had settled in British ports. After the Second World War, British textile mills and foundries were short of workers, and these early links helped others follow. Then came the Mangla Dam on the Jhelum river, built in the 1960s under the Indus Waters Treaty. Its lake flooded the old town of Mirpur and many villages, displacing over a hundred thousand people. Some of the compensation paid for passages to Britain.

The migrants settled in mill and factory towns such as Bradford, Birmingham, Oldham and Luton. Men came first and families followed, especially after Britain tightened immigration laws in the 1960s and 70s. People of Mirpuri origin now make up a large share of British Pakistanis. Money sent home built new houses in Mirpur, which is sometimes nicknamed "Little England".
sum: The movement of tens of thousands of people from the Mirpur district of Pakistani-administered Kashmir to Britain, which grew sharply from about 1960.
